maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, February 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King that a select committee be appointed to examine and report on the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living, and matters pertaining thereto.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday night when this debate adjourned I had said a good deal, and I am not going to repeat anything that I said at that time. To pick up the discussion where I left off, I suggest to the house that the government was not smart when it refused to accept the amendments proposed by the official opposition and by the C.C.F. group. All that the amendments suggested was to broaden the scope of the committee, to give it latitude with regard to bringing in some recommendation.
If the committee is restricted so that it cannot do anything, then it serves very little purpose and the investigation will not mean very much. I have in mind the industrial relations committee which was handling a serious and urgent problem. I know how it functioned; I know of the restrictions which were placed on it. It had no legal status, no right to recommend, no right to file a minority report. It was merely a matter of getting something backstage and out of the mind of the public.
Had the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the government accepted the amendments proposed, in effect they would have been tying every group in the house to the committee, but by refusing to permit any latitude whatsoever, as suggested by the opposition, the several groups in the house are placed in the position of having to consider whether they are being logical or not in accepting membership on the committee if and when it is set up. I consider that the last amendment of the C.C.F. group was a proper one and that the house should have been permitted to vote on it. Believing that, I am going to read it again to refresh the memory of some hon. members who were home on Thursday and Friday. The amendment reads as follows:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
this house is of the opinion that the present crisis demands and the people of Canada want not a parliamentary committee but action by the government to restore price controls and subsidies.
Prices Committee

The reason I say this is the motion that the house should be voting on is that this is the issue in the country, whether the government likes it or not-not the matter of setting up a committee. Every hon. member, irrespective of the side of the house on which he sits, if he is honest with himself will tell the house that from all sections of the public in his own constituency-farmers, church organizations, Canadian legion, non-political organizations- all of them have been submitting resolution after resolution to hon. members demanding the reimposition of price controls and the reenactment of the subsidy arrangement to halt the trend in the inflationary spiral that is now on. That matter should have been voted on in this house, because that is the issue. But' it was not done, and the government will have to take the responsibility for it.
In my opinion the setting up of a committee would be all right provided action were taken first to try to hold the line where it is at the present time; then the committee could investigate and ascertain the reason for the present inflation and the matter of profiteering, so called. But that was not done, and the responsibility for the delay in getting something done will have to rest with those who voted against our proposal to have action taken immediately.
In the matter of increase of price-and the increases have been drastic in the last four or five months-in my opinion it is not an accident. The Minister of Finance told the country, not in this house but through the press and over the air, that the present trend in prices was going according to plan and that they would strike a certain level and then level off. If the inflation we have today is planned inflation, then we should cease wasting time in the house discussing the matter. Personally I believe it is.
My conception of the present situation is that there is such a tight integration between the economies of Canada and the United States that price levels in this country are going to reach the levels prevailing south of the line. In my opinion that is the trend. But I would suggest to members of this house that they also take note of what is happening in the United States according to today's press. The stock market is getting shaky and prices are beginning to fall. That is the initial step towards unemployment and depression. It is not a good sign, and the time is not far distant when that trend will put the "not wanted" signs up on plant and factory gates.
What is the reason? The reason in my opinion is that the Marshall plan in the United States has not got under way as soon as it

should, with the result that purchasing power in Europe is nil, goods are beginning to pile up in the United States, the market is getting shaky, prices are beginning to fall, and the next thing in the United States will be depression and unemployment.
I urge the people in charge of the economy of this country, that is to say the government, to watch things in the United States, not to follow events blindly, because in my opinion the thing will tailspin over there unless Truman gets the support of his government and the reimposition of controls and subsidies towards which he has been working for some considerable time now.
I do not think a committee investigating this matter in Canada at this time is the proper kind of action. It is too serious. Something must be done about it quickly. What will they investigate in the matter of profiteering? In my opinion there is no such thing as profiteering in Canada. Under the present system anyone in Canada who has something to sell is legitimately entitled to charge what the traffic will bear, and in the present trend that is indicated clearly. Butter for example was selling at 70 cents a pound. The government undertook to put a ceiling on it, but it did not put a ceiling on it. It put a sky on it. It was jumped from 70 cents, and a ceiling of 73 cents was put on.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: That is not true.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: It is true. So when your committee sits and takes evidence, where will be the line of demarcation? How will you determine what profiteering is? When is a man a profiteer? Under the present scheme he is allowed to charge as much as he can get. There is no law in this country that will enable the courts to determine when a man is profiteering. There may be exorbitant prices, but there is no law that says a man cannot charge and get for what he is selling, for any commodity he is handling, whatever he can get under the present scheme of things.

You have no fixed profits. That is one thing we have urged in this house time and again. We have been urging that in addition to fixing prices and regulating wages, profits also should be fixed. Profits are one of the big factors today in this country-one of the factors that have got us into the mess we are now in-because they are uncontrolled until such time as the government is prepared to lay down some definite regulations with regard to the margin of profit anyone is permitted to make, taking anything in excess of

Prices Committee
that in the form of excess profits. But you have nothing to investigate anywhere, and you cannot bring into this house anything that [DOT]will condemn anyone in this country for any price he 13 charging.
In the hands of the government just now there is all the necessary machinery. There is the Combines Investigation Act. This matter has all been gone over before and there is no necessity for me to go over it again, but I strongly urge that if you set up a committee it should go into the matter thoroughly. It is not a bad idea to have a committee that will go thoroughly into the whole economy, overhaul it, and bring some evidence into the house on the necessity for legislation to control and regulate things in this country in the interests of all the people. But in the meantime, with the present upward trend of things in this country, action should be taken by the government, even if it be a temporary action, to reimpose controls and subsidies in order to hold the line where it is at the present time.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
-unless I am provoked into saying more than I had1 intended to say. I believe this motion has been introduced largely because in the house and the country there is a great deal of confusion on fundamental principles. I believe that the public generally-including most of the members of this house, have not yet a proper conception of fundamental principles. I do not think we have yet reached the stage where we have clearly defined in our minds what constitutes a properly functioning democracy. I shall try in a few moments to give my views as to what constitutes a properly functioning democracy in relation to this particular resolution.
First of all I think we shall have to spend a little time in defining the duties and responsibilities of the electors as such; then we shall have to try to come to some conclusion as to what is our particular duty as members of parliament and what generally speaking is the duty of the government. If we can come to an agreement on these particular aspects of the matter we shall make more progress in considering resolutions and motions such as the one now before us.
I think the confusion which exists in the public mind arises because there is not a clear differentiation between the duties of citizens as such and the duties of members of parliament. Member after member has risen in this house and said that the people of Canada demand' price control. As members we have been receiving resolutions, letters and telegrams from labour bodies, organizations of various kinds, and individuals, demanding that we support the reimposition of price controls. I wish to say, as I have said in reply to those who have written to me and telegraphed me, that I do not think that the

Prices Committee
people who write these resolutions and letters have a proper understanding of their duties. I do not think the public ought to be concerned about the methods that are used to achieve results. Generally speaking what the public wants is a higher standard of living, or a lower cost of living. It is a result they want. They are not concerned with controls as such. Control is a method1 by which they think a certain result can be obtained. In my opinion the only reason people throughout this country are saying they want price controls is that they are taking direction from a lot of misguided leaders. These are people who have assumed1 or have been given leadership ini labour and other organizations here, there and1 everywhere, and they are saying to the people, "We want price controls. Ask for them." So they have a chorus of people all over the country from coast to coast saying, "We want price controls," whereas it is not price controls they want at all, but rather a higher standard of living, a lower cost of living. That is what they ought to be concerned about.
I feel that if the great majority of people in this country were able to differentiate between results and methods we would not have this resolution before us at the present time. If the people were organized as a functioning democracy they would be demanding of the members of this house, particularly those on the government side, that they produce certain results, and if they cannot produce these results they should resign. First of all, I believe, people will have to learn to distinguish between results and methods; then they will have to organize themselves in such a way that they can effectively demand the results they wish. At the present time in this country, and probably in every country in the world, the people are not so organized. They are divided into parties in a dozen ways, and the parties are quarrelling and quibbling over methods. One says we want price controls; another says we need socialization and nationalization; another says we need monetary reform, and the people are divided over methods while methods are something about which the people should not be concerned at all. So I think one of the first things the people must do in this country is to learn to distinguish between results and methods, and then organize in such a way that they can obtain from their democratic institutions the results they want.
As long as we are operating under the political party system I feel that the government has the responsibility for bringing about the results the people want. As far as the
information which may be obtained by this committee is concerned, the government has adequate facilities at the present time for obtaining all the information it needs to give the people the results they want, so I think the committee really is superfluous. Yet I am not going to oppose it. If this committee, which is to be purely a fact-finding body, did nothing else than show the people that the charges the C.C.F. and the communists in this country are making are unfounded, it will be well worth while.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), who has just resumed his seat, in a manner typical of C.C.F. speakers, harangued us once more on the subject of profits alleged to have been made by corporations and companies. If the committee does nothing but indicate and establish that the high cost of living is not due to exorbitant profits, I think it will be well worth while.
The hon. member who preceded me made some statements about the profits the packing plants were making at the expense of the farmers. He was interrupted by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), who asked whether he considered that the farmers were making exorbitant profits, but the hon. member for Cape Breton South adroitly sidestepped that question. Here is something which may interest the C.C.F. members, who are constantly making the charge that high prices are due to excessive profits. During the packing plant strike last fall an item appeared in our western newspapers as to the profits the packing plants were making. I cannot vouch for the accuracy of this statement, but at least it is what was said by one packing plant. This item was headed, "Packing plants claim 35 cents profit on $100," and this is the way they itemize the cost content of the commodities they process.
A chart released by Burns & Company Limited shows how every $100 of their income from packing house operations in 1946 was distributed.
$81.42 went to the producers, for livestock, poultry, cream, etc.; $10.03 were wages to employees. Supplies for packaging finished products used up $2.70. Power, transportation and advertising claimed $3.82. Depreciation of plant and machinery amounted to 99 cents. Interest was 31 cents (bonds, 21 cents; bank, 10 cents). Income and property taxes took 38 cents. Profit was left at 35 cents on every one hundred dollars.
This appeared last October, and I imagine other companies have made similar statements. I should like to see the C.C.F., through those who serve them on this committee, try to establish that this is not true, that the profits were far in excess of 35 cenis

I was just saying that I thought the Prime Minister and his associates retained power in this country largely through tricking the electorate into voting for them. I should like to give what I consider an instance of that. The Prime Minister, unless he suffers from a lapse of memory, must recall his own statement away back in 1935, supposed to have been made in Saskatoon. He said:
Canada is faced with a great battle between the money power and the power of the people, a battle which will be waged in the next parliament. I plead for a sweeping Liberal victory to carry out my policy of public control of currency and credit. Until the control of currency and credit is returned to the government, .all talk of the sovereignty of parliament and democracy is idle and futile.
Those are very noble sentiments, and no doubt the Prime Minister and1 his supporters will claim that those proposals have been implemented. That may be their conception of it, but it certainly is not mine and I doubt whether it is the conception of the people of Canada. In the light of that statement I will go so far as to say that the Prime Minister and those who support him have betrayed1 the people of this country. They led the people to believe that they were going to do battle with the money power. If they did do battle they certainly dtid not win out but rather succumbed to the money power. Until the people organize themselves more effectively they will be at the mercy of party politicians. The Prime Minister led the people to believe that they were going to get results, and he indicated the means 'by which those results would be attained. maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: They fought on the side of the money power instead of against it, and are still doing so.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: So far as the people are concerned I do not think they are to blame for the present circumstances. They have done their duty and are still prepared to do it. They are willing to produce tremendous quantities of goods and services. They have the necessary knowledge and facilities to raise production far in excess of what it is now, but because the Liberal party under the leadership of the Prime Minister have not carried out their own program the people at the present time are being prevented from doing what they otherwise would do. The murderous taxation imposed on this country at the present time is discouraging production in every possible way. Surely the greatest contribution that can be made to attacking inflation is to increase production, but when taxation is such that the farmer, the worker and everybody else is discouraged from increasing production how can we effectively combat inflation? So I say that the responsibility is largely that of the government and nobody else. They are pursuing a financial policy which is not in the interests of the people of Canada, and I suggest that they do a little conscience-searching and look at some of their own statements in the past with a view to carrying them out. If they will only do that it will go a long way towards taking care of the situation, and they will certainly receive my support. But they do net seem to be willing to do so, therefore they will simply have to take the consequences.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: No, the people will.

speechtext:
In conclusion I wish to put on record a few sentences from a radio broadcast I made in reply to those who sent me telegrams and letters asking me to support price control. I do so in order to indicate my stand on this particular question. I said this:
I appreciate all the letters and telegrams which I have received from electors of my ridmg expressing concern about the high cost of living. If such communications indicate nothing else, they indicate that the people responsible for them are aware that they have *a member of parliament and that thev have a right to expect him to serve them. This is as it should be and I appreciate this demonstration of democratic action.
I have a criticism, however, of these letters and telegrams tand it is this: Most of them demand that I as the member of parliament for Jasper-Edson support the reimposition of price controls in Canada. Such demands arise from a confusion as to what are the duties of a citizen and what are the duties of a member of parliament. As I see it, it is the duty of the electors to demand results and not to indicate the methods by which those results are to be obtained. What the electors of Jasper-Edson, along with all other Canadians, really want is a higher standard of living. I am cer-

Prices Committee
tain that if they knew that a higher standard of living could be secured without price controls, they would never demand of me that I support the reimposition of price controls. I am personally convinced that Canadians can enjoy their just share of national production without the government resorting to a system of price controls. I would go further and say that a system of price controls would retard and restrict production, which in turn would lower the amount of goods which could be made available for Canadian consumption.
Time will not permit me to elaborate on this statement but I consider it to be true.
My suggestion therefore is that the electors of Jasper-Edson, along with all other electors, would conform, much more to democratic principles if they would demand results of their members of parliament rather than suggest methods by which they think those results can be achieved. Price control is a method and may not be a desirable method. This is a matter for experts to decide and one about which neither the electors nor members of parliament as such should be concerned.
I would suggest, therefore, that in the future, all demands directed towards me and other members of parliament be in the nature of demands for results rather than for the methods to be employed.
Let the electors unite in a demand for a drastic reduction and ultimate abolition of all dominion taxation and they will strike the most effective blow possible at the high cost of living and will at the same time be demonstrating truly democratic practice.
That is part of the reply which I gave, and that is my attitude on the subject of control. In addition, I suggest that the time is opportune for us to consider a little more seriously some of the fundamentals to which I have referred. I am satisfied that if we do that as a nation it will not be long before the people get the results that they really want.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to talk very much about this question of controls, because it is quite apart from the subject matter of this resolution. My hon. friends to the left have advocated the reimposition of controls and subsidies. It is not just as simple as that. If you keep making statements long enough and make them plausible enough, as they have been doing, you can get many people to believe what you say. I do not intend to discuss that question now.
Like everybody else, Mr. Speaker, I do not need to say that I realize the cost of living is high and also that the cost has steadily risen over the last year. I do not think anybody will say that that is not so. The question before the house at the present time is a resolution to set up a committee to inquire into, not the cost of living, but the recent rise in the cost of living.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) drew attention to the fact that in 1919 a similar resolution was introduced by Sir Thomas White. I shall deal with that later on. The
Prime Minister said that it was passed without any debate, and I gathered from his remarks that he thought this resolution should have been passed with very little debate. He said that it was a similar resolution. Sometimes resolutions are not just what they seem on the surface. When one goes into the question of what resolutions mean, what their implications are, he may find that they are not as simple as they seem. In examining the whole thing I found that out to my own satisfaction.
I make no apologies for taking part in this debate. I suppose that I, as well as other members of the opposition, will be criticized by the Prime Minister for the delay which has been caused in the last three or four days in debating the resolution. I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that any blame which may be attached to us for taking part in this debate in the few days that have elapsed since the resolution was introduced will not be nearly as much as the blame which will be attached to the government and to the Prime Minister if they delay action until the committee has reported without recommendations, has reported some of the facts, since it will be many months before anything is done, before any information will come from the committee so that the government and the country will be able to take action as a result.
My concern in taking part in this debate is the concern I have for the people who have to pay the prices of today. I am concerned especially with the people on fixed income-pensioners, superannuated people, widows, and the like.
What are the terms of the resolution? It reads in part:
That a select committee of this house be appointed to examine and to report from time to time as to:
(a)	the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living;
(b)	prices which have been raised above levels justified by increased costs;
(c)	rises in prices due to the acquiring, accumulating or withholding from sale by any persons, firms or corpora; ions of any goods beyond amounts reasonably required for the ordinary purposes of their businesses.
I shall not read it all. The resolution goes on:
That the committee shall consist of Messrs: Beaudry, Cleaver, Fleming, Homuth, Johnston, Knowles, Lesage, Martin, Maybank, Mayhew, McCubbin, Merritt, Nicholson, Pinard, Smith (Calgary West), Winters, and that standing order 65 be suspended in relation thereto.
The committee consists of one cabinet minister, four parliamentary assistants and five members of the Liberal party, a total of nine Liberal members; four Conservative members, two C.C.F. members and one Social Credit
Prices Committee

member. That includes all of the opposition. I shall have something to say about that later.
In introducing the resolution the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 744 of Hansard:
I might begin by saying that I believe all hon. members of the house are agreed that the question of the recent rise in prices, particularly of the increase in the cost of living, is a matter of nation-wide concern.
The Prime Minister's statement is accurate, to say the least. Not only are members of the House of Commons concerned with the recent rise, not only is it nation-wide, Mr. Speaker, but it extends over the past year, as illustrated by the following figures which I intend to put on Hansard, since they have been obtained from the January copy of the Labour Gazette. These are the figures month by month adjusted to base 100 for August, 1939. The January increase was -8 points; February 1-1; March 1-7; April 2-4; May 1-8; June TO; July -7; August 2-8; September 2-8; October 1-4; November 2-5 and December 2-3. It does not look to me as if there has been any considerable recent rise. The increase has been pretty steady over the year. The total rise is 21-3 points in the year, and the average was almost 1-8 point per month.
Food increased from 145-5 on January 1, 1946, to 182-2 on January 1 of this year, or an increase of 36-7. As I said before, it is not just a recent rise that is concerning the people, but the rise that has taken place over this year. I am surprised, as I am sure the country is surprised, that the Prime Minister used that word "recent". I know that the house and the country would like to know why that word "recent" was inserted in the resolution. They appreciate the significance of it, because it will effectually prevent any inquiry into the effect of government policy on the cost of living. The Prime Minister went on to say, at page 744 of Hansard:
This afternoon I do not intend to go into the question of the causes of the rises in prices, or of possible remedies, but merely to bring forward a motion on one related matter which is part of the government's program in dealing with this large question.
In view of the nation-wide concern over the increases in the cost of living it is surprising to me that the Prime Minister did not go into the question of the causes. I think the country is disappointed that some statement of this kind was not made by the Prime Minister at this time. He has had long experience in these matters. In 1920 he had no hesitation in telling the country that he knew- all about it, what the causes were and all that sort of thing, and what he would do about it when he was returned to power.
	'
It seems to me that he is strangely silent now, and also strangely silent on other matters relating to government policy.
This resolution, the Prime Minister says, pertains to one of a series of measures which the government has adopted and other measures that the government will bring forward later. Mark that word. The government will bring forward measures later. But the people of the country do not want a committee; they want some kind of action on the part of the government.
What other measure has the government up its sleeve which it will bring forward later? It does not do the people any good to have these measures brought forward later. The Prime Minister says that for obvious reasons some parts of the program could not be disclosed, and then he refers to taxation proposals which he says cannot be disclosed before the budget is brought down.
What a change of attitude has taken place on the part of the government! How selfrighteous they are all of a sudden. Go back to November 1947 and they did not hesitate to disclose and to bring into force by order in council some of the most drastic legislation that has ever been perpetrated on the people of Canada, when parliament was not sitting, by way of the prohibition of imports and also the imposition of the twenty-five per cent excise tax.
If the government have a policy about things they intend to bring forward later, why not bring it into force now? Why not bring in a budget now, so that whatever tax reductions may be given to the people may be had now and not two or three months from now? Why not give some relief at once by reducing the eight per cent sales tax and the twenty-five per cent excise tax?
I recall when the Prime Minister in the election campaign of 1935 went from coast to coast and fairly howled against the sales tax, telling the people at that time what an iniquitous thing it was and what he would do if elected. He would cut the tax-cut it out, I think it was. But what did1 he do? Right after being elected, after getting a majority and coming back, in the budget of 1936 the tax was not cut but was increased from six to eight per cent. I have no confidence in promises of that kind as to what the government will do by reason of something they have up their sleeve.
Promptness is what is wanted in this connection, and now is the time to take action. A reduction in these taxes would have a great effect on the cost of living, and the responsibility is the government's. I would like them now, more especially the Prime Minister, to

Prices Committee
spring into action, although that seems funny language to use about this government. If he really meant what he said in connection with the sales tax in 1935, about the iniquity of the sales tax, and if he meant 'his previous promises to reduce the tax or cut it out, if the promise was not one for election purposes, as he definitely established in the pre-war years, the Prime Minister would have his Minister of Finance bring down a temporary budget, now while the house is in session, and materially reduce the eight per cent sales tax and the twenty-five per cent excise tax. It would be far better to do something like that.
The government imposed' other taxes by order in council when parliament was not sitting, and they could take action now while parliament is sitting. Why should they not bring in something of that kind? It is estimated at the present time that they will have a surplus of between S700 million and $800 million. Well, why not take some of that and give the people a little relief?
Talk about the high cost of living! When you think of it, every man, woman and child in this country pay taxes on the average of $187. Think of it-S187 per capita. That certainly has a lot to do with the cost of living. Take a family of four and multiply that amount four times and see what it comes to.
Another thing that enters into the high cost of living is the taxes caused' by the number of people in the employ of the government, and that should be taken care of.
Let us take an example of the working of the sales -tax. In 1939 the sales tax of eight per cent meant $8 on every $100 worth of goods purchased. These same goods now cost S150 and the tax on these goods is $12-the very same goods that were bought in 1939. That amounts to 12 per cent tax on the same goods bought in 1939. Not only that, but the eight per cent tax pyramids many times on the cost of the necessities of life of the people; it is eight per cent on the labour content of an article all the way from the raw material to the finished product. As a consequence at each stage those engaged in the operations have of necessity to charge more for the wages of their labour.
So there is a pyramiding. Therefore the sales tax cost content of the article now would probably be more like 20 per cent, or an equivalent of about 30 per cent in 1939. Government policy is responsible for a considerable portion of the high cost of living, as can be easily seen through the spiral of tax increases.
Now I come to the words of the Prime Minister as reported at page 745 of Hansard where he said:
In 1919 Sir Thomas White, who if I recollect aright was then minister of finance, introduced a motion for the establishment of a committee on the cost of living. He did so by a motion very similar to the one I am introducing at the present time.
As I said before, he calls that a very similar motion. Let us see what the motion was that was introduced by Sir Thomas White in 1919. These are the words:
That a special committee of the house . . . be appointed for the purpose of inquiring forthwith as to the prices charged throughout Canada for foodstuffs, clothing, fuel and other necessaries of life ... to report to the house from time to time the result of their inquiry with any recommendations they may make with a view to effecting a reduction in such prices and rentals.
Although the Prime Minister calls his motion very similar to that one, the only similarity that I see is that they are both resolutions. This committee set up in 1919 were not limited in scope; they were not limited to the examination of recent prices. They had a direct, definite function to fulfil. More important, they had a duty to report their recommendations to the house, so that the report with recommendations could be debated in the House of Commons in a democratic way. The committee here have no power and no teeth. They have no power to make recommendations to the wartime prices and trade board, to the combines investigation commission or anyone else. It is true that the individual members of the committee will have the power, and the right I suppose, to go to any of these government bodies and demand some kind of action, but how much that would mean or how much satisfaction they would get I do not know. By the rules of the house and the very nature of the committee, parliament will be prevented from making recommendations or debating matters under discussion before the committee.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) said he hoped that the scope of this committee would be kept within practical limits; otherwise we shall lose the substance by grasping at the shadow. That is exactly what will happen, Mr. Speaker. I should like to ask the minister what he means by practical results-no recommendations-inquire into only the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living. I think the minister has plenty of cause to fear, because shadows will be all that will emerge from the committee. Let us go into what will be examined by the committee. One at a time, please; I am ready to listen. A week ago today the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) brought into the house a motion asking for the appointment of a parliamentary committee to study the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living. In the period of that week we have listened as attentively as patience would allow to a tirade of speeches, about which, were I permitted to criticize,, I would have something to say. However, I am hoping the house will be as generous to me as I try to be to it when I refrain from criticizing both the form and content of those speeches.
I look now at the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), and I must say he inspires me to say that we did hear a good speech here and there. His was one of them. He knows I am an admirer of his, and he will not be surprised when I extend to him this compliment.
But we heard many examples of circuses. On our side we heard it said that it is not right to ride two horses at the same time-a most profound discovery! Then, on the other side, that it is not proper for two horses to go against each other in opposite directions. Then we listened to the statement attributed to Barnum and Bailey, that you can fool some of the people some of the time. These great sociologists, these great statements about Bamum and Bailey-and I regret the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) is not in his seat at the present time to see what a monumental statement he has made, and what a profound contribution he has offered in the debate! We were threatened with sit-down strikes and exclusions, and one gentleman of the cloth got us down to the boogie-woogie basis: "Open the Door Richard"; "You Can Have Her; I Don't Want Her; She's Too Fat For Me". And he might have added "Bungle, bungle, bungle; I don't want to leave the jungle", which perhaps would have been equally appropriate.
We have listened in the hope that these gentlemen would balk themselves out, or that someone would come forward with a definite and complete proposal which could be put into effect. But that did not happen. One can divide the objections into three categories. The official opposition wanted a bigger and better committee, with powers to report and recommend. In the second place, they say that the present government agencies should look into this matter of the high cost of living. Someone suggested that the removal of the sales tax would be a remedy, although the

Financial Post has pointed out how absurd this would be for the national economy of Canada.
And when a bigger and better committee with powers to recommend is suggested, I am free to anticipate, in the same manner as hon. members opposite, what would happen. Not one of them understands the contents of the bill to be brought down. All they have before them is a motion stating that the government wants to appoint a committee to investigate into the causa causans, into the definite and absolute cause for the rising prices.

Oh, we remember 1925 and 1926 when Mr. Stevens, later minister of trade and commerce in the Bennett cabinet, one who shared ministerial responsiblity and was supposed to speak for the government of Canada, made certain charges on the floor of this house against the then minister of customs, Mr. Boivin, in regard to prices which caused a split between him and Mr. Bennett, with the result that the destruction party,-or was it the reconstruction party?

was formed.

Prices Committee
When the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, said that the investigation should be conducted under the Combines Investigation Act, he was right, because a minister of the crown had made definite and categorical charges. Mr. Stevens said:	This
is what is actually happening; and he indicated where it happened and who was responsible. He made specific charges and asked for a committee of inquiry. But today the story is entirely different. No one on the floor of this house has made a definite charge as to where the misfortune, the difficulty, the ill, the trouble lies. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), whom I respect for his reasonableness and fairness, will confirm my statement that the Combines Investigation Act was meant to be an investigating agency of the government, to be applied with respect to a specific commodity in regard to which there is an artificial combine between producers and distributors to raise or lower prices artificially. But when a situation arises affecting the whole national economy, when a price rise takes place from Vancouver to Halifax, though to a much less extent than the rise amongst our neighbours to the south, we say that we are going to ascertain the primary cause of that rise and, when found, parliament will apply the remedy. The Prime Minister consequently is right this time just as he was right in 1034.
The Progressive Conservative party suggest no remedy whatsoever. The leader of the official opposition discussed the removal of the sales tax and the hon. member for Lake Centre followed and repeated the same remedy. The Financial Post came out and completely refuted the statement that removal of the sales tax would be the remedy. It would help the manufacturers; it would help the distributors. speechtext:
You got to the wheel in
England and, good heavens, that little island is melting away as if it had never existed; so much so that Attlee, Bevin and Morrison have come out lately and said to the workers what no capitalist employer would dare say. Mr. Attlee said: "You must work more hours; more production and more work, if you do not want to face starvation and bankruptcy." You would not dare repeat that on the floor here, although you turn around and say, " Look what we are doing for the people."
Speaking is the cheapest form of obtaining votes, but it is not a fundamental principle. My hon. friends say, " We want controls." Speaker after speaker of the C,C.F. has risen in his place and said, "Give us controls and subsidies; give us; give us." I would ask any one of the hon. members, at what point shall the controls start? Where shall they begin and where shall they end? To whom shall subsidies be given at this juncture of our economy? It is all right to say, "Give us controls." If I thought that was the remedy, I would ask for the same thing.
What does the Prime Minister require from this committee? If controls are the remedy, we shall give controls. If controls are necessary

Prices Committee
we shall impose them; but where? Shall they be imposed on the farmer who has raised the price of his produce 200 per cent above the 1939 level? Shall it be given to him? Shall a control be imposed on the food producers whose costs have gone up 200 per cent?
The farmer is already controlled in the price of everything he sells today.
These things are not fundamental-	,
Come on out in the country .and say that.

I hear speeches about the
poor farmers; the next thing we are going to do for the farmer is to chew the food and put it into his mouth. Don't tell me-
Liberal policy.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: What does the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) think -of that?
He shakes his head.

I hope the time taken up ini cross-fire by the hon. gentlemen will not be counted on my time. If you take any chart, and if you are objectively sincere in your statement, you will find that the cost of food, judged on 1939 levels, has risen 200 per cent. I have a chart which was published in the New York Times last Sunday which I am willing to produce and deposit with the house, and let any hon. member refute that statement. If you are thinking of your constituency, perhaps you will be able to get a few more farmer votes. Then, go ahead and do it, but the truth must be faced. I represent .an urban constituency, and if we have to pay seventy-one cents a pound for butter it is because in this house you are hollered down, you are told you must not speak about the farmer. Well, now, somebody has to tell the farmer that we know what we are paying today. Industrials have gone up 162 per cent, according to the Nejv York Times; but if we are given controls, shall the controls be imposed today at the present levels? Would the C.C.F. suggest that? Would they impose subsidies? Would they offer subsidies to the farmers whose products have risen 200 per cent? Apparently that is not practical; that is not acceptable; that is not desirable; and from what we have seen of what has happened in England and from what we have seen happen in Soviet Russia, controls and subsidies are the shortest way to bankruptcy.
If Prime Minister Attlee had to come out and say, "We need1 more production, we want
our workers not to ask for a higher increase in wages-" and) these are the words of Attlee. If Bevin had to use the same language, if Sir Stafford Cripps had to ask for it, what would happen to the economy of Canada; if the C.C.F. were in power here? They would have to impose the same conditions. England is today spending one billion and a half in subsidies, and they do not know how to get rid of them. Consequently I do not see that the suggestion is practical. I read in a letter published in the Citizen that milk is as expensive in Scotland as it is in Canada. It is selling at about fourteen cents a quart over there, and I am willing to produce that letter from a visitor to England to that effect. Therefore, when you insist that the Canadian people be given subsidies and that controls be put on the economy of the country you are misleading yourself and you are misleading the people of Canada.
Alternately you say, "We produced an amendment and if you do not accept our amendment we may go on strike." I think hon. gentlemen are much too public-minded to make statements of that kind. They know their obligation to the country, and if this government is wrong in presenting any kind of remedy it is best for hon. gentlemen who are on the committee to fight from inside and remedy the conditions, but not threaten to go on strike. As a matter of fact, I do not think they will go on strike. Personally I think they will be vocal inside and outside of parliament so that their electors will read what action they have taken.
The Social Credit party object to the word "recently" in the motion. I respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that the word "recently" is appropriate, as you will see, and I recommend the financial chart of the New York Times to hon. members, which indicates definitely that the cost of living has risen sharply since 1946, not only in Canada but in the United States'. The same thing applies to England and1 to the other countries. If it has risen since 1946 and we are now in the first months of 1948 it has risen recently, I submit to the leader of the third opposition party. Hon. gentlemen know what happened in this world cataclysm from which we have just emerged and the general economic dislocation which has taken place.
When the Prime Minister, speaking in this house, said that conditions have developed beyond the control of Canada, a roar of laughter went up from the Conservatives. What would actually have happened if Canada had been an airtight compartment administering its own economy, and having
Prices Committee

complete control, without relationship to other nations? Would the cost of living have been as successfully coped with as it has been until now? The demand for commodities by other countries, whether or not they are able to pay, the necessity for these commodities, has produced a world situation which has confounded the economy of Canada, and if we are honest with ourselves we shall find that the cost of living in Canada has risen less than in any other country.
There is no country that can equal Canada in the administration of the Canadian government. Of course we all want to better conditions in Canada. I do not suspect that any hon. member had not the finest motives in speaking on the motion. But we must realize the facts that face us in the conditions under which we live. If it had been a Canadian question entirely, and one could say that there was a difference in the selling price as between commodities, a difference in operations, in cost of production, and that some middleman or some combine had caused this difference, the situation would not be the same. But it is not solely a Canadian situation. Yet this government had the courage; this government, which managed the country during the worst years that we have passed through, had the courage to come forward and say, "We will appoint a committee and if there is any remedy"-they did not say it would not be applied-"whether it is the sales tax, or the Combines Investigation Act, or the wartime prices and trade board, or controls, or whether it is subsidies, we will apply it."
There is nothing before this house so contentious that it should have taken a whole week of discussion. I appreciate the generosity of the leader of this house, the generosity of the Speaker in allowing everyone to wander wherever he wanted. Hon. members could speak about every subject they desired. That was tolerated and accepted. They tried one's patience sometimes, but it was acceptable. I repeat, however, that there is nothing so contentious in the motion as to require such a lengthy discussion. If the report of the committee is not acceptable to the house we shall have ample time to discuss the remedies that are to be applied. But it is this government that first introduced controls and subsidies. It was not any other group that did it. We did it successfully when it was necessary, and this government will cariy on and see that the cost of living is compatible with the earning conditions of the worker in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. II ARK NESS (Calgary East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. 
Hartt) seems a bit confused as to what the motion is for. He appears to think it is preparatory to introducing a bill or something of that kind. However, he is no more confused in regard to this issue than he appears to be in connection with any other question which he attempted to discuss. The only thing he seems to be certain about is Barnum and Bailey and I suggest that he join that organization. I am sure they would furnish an appropriate setting for his talents.
I will go there to see my *hon. friend.

Speaking to the motion, I should like to make some comments on the speech of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) on Tuesday last. Such comment is particularly applicable, because I believe the whole tenor of 'his speech is typical of the attitude the government is taking on this motion to set up a committee to study prices. The general effect of the minister's speech was to misinterpret what has happened and thus mislead the house and the country. The minister attempted to prove that farmers and farm organizations are well satisfied with the agricultural policies which he has followed and with the food contracts into which he has entered. To prove his case he read a letter from the Canadian poultry council expressing satisfaction with the new egg contract with Great Britain. Later, some doubt was cast on how far that council represented the poultry growers, but in any event the production of eggs is not one of the major agricultural activities of this country, not that it is not important.
This was followed by a resolution passed at the Canadian Federation of Agriculture meeting in Brockville some ten days ago. If anyone reads this resolution I think he will admit that it does nothing to 'help the minister's case. This was followed again by another resolution in connection with livestock, a resolution which is definitely condemnatory of the government and its policies. Why the minister thought it was the reverse I do not know; I presume it was wishful thinking on his part. I should like to read this resolution, which is reported at page 803 of Hansard:
Whereas during the past year there has been a serious decline in hog production and in cattle slaughterings, which if not checked, may result in an actual shortage of supplies of meat on the domestic market. . .
If there is anything favourable to the government in that statement I do not know what it is.	.
And whereas the embargo against the shipment of livestock to the United States has acted as a most effective price control on livestock and livestock products;

Prices Committee
Resolved that this meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture strongly protest the reimposition of further price controls on livestock and livestock products, unless these are accompanied by a policy of over-all control of prices of those goods and services which constitute the farmers' production costs.
The minister tried to make it appear that that resolution approves the policies he has been carrying into effect. I submit that everything in it is a condemnation of what the minister has been doing.
The minister next attempted to show that the beef producers were in accord with his policies and ideas. Actually, nothing could be farther from the truth. He went into a long rigmarole and tried to confuse the issue, but the telegram he read from the National Council of Canadian Beef Producers is a condemnation of his policy, if anything is. This is the telegram:
Resolved that this council go on record as approving the restoration of the right to private export of cattle and to all the benefits accruing therefrom.
This resolution is interesting, because the question arose at Lethbridge on the day following the meeting which the Minister of Agriculture had with the beef men of Alberta. I should like to read a few extracts from the newspaper account of that meeting to indicate what the livestock men really think of the minister's policies and so forth. This is headed:
Cattlemen applaud secession threat.
Stockmen wiring gov't to restore private export.
Minister of Agriculture gets some boos after chiding westerners at Lethbridge.
This is from the Calgary Herald of January 16. The report then goes on:
A request that western Canadian cattle producers join with him in demanding that the west secede from the east if the dominion government persists in its decision to keep the United States market closed to Canadian commercial cattle, was made by George Ross, of Aden, when he addressed the Friday morning session of the western stock growers association.
Mr. Ross, who is chairman of the western section of the council of Canadian beef producers, was speaking to a resolution which asked that delegates go on record as asking for "restoration of private export of cattle and participation in all benefits accruing therefrom."
In other words, this is the very resolution which the minister read into the record, attempting to show that it was favourable to him and his policies. The report goes on:
Mr. Ross said that he was cognizant of the seriousness of the statement which he had made but he felt that the situation was such that drastic measures were required.
His threat of secession was received with loud applause.
Mr. Ross has led the fight for restoration of the United States market over a period of years.
The speakers who followed were unanimous in support of the resolution-
That is this resolution which the minister read the other day.

although a few of them said that further representations to the government appeared useless in face of the definite stand made by the Right Hon. James G. Gardiner Thursday night that there was no possibility of the market being reopened for the present.
I do not think there is much use in my reading any more of these extracts.

That is enough.
Mr. HARIvNESS: I have one other here:
The cattlemen sat in grim silence as the minister outlined in detail the government's agricultural policy as it related to the beef industry . . .
That is enough.

That is the kind of thing that happened there. The livestock men who were there were definitely opposed to the government. Yet the Minister of Agriculture comes into this house and reads a resolution they pass and tries to make it appear that they approved his policy. The situation is really rather a ridiculous one.
In addition to trying to make actually one of the most violent protests against his policy appear as a stand in favour of it, the minister totally disregarded the numerous resolutions he has had from influential farm bodies condemning his policies and asking for a change. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) and I put on the record before Christmas the stand of the Alberta Farmers' Union in connection with this government's agricultural policies. Perhaps the minister has forgotten what the stand of that body was, and I should like to refresh his memory in connection with it. This is the convention program of the Alberta Farmers' Union held on December 1 to 5, 1947. It is filled with resolutions condemning this government's policies. I will take up the time of the house to read only parts of one or two. The most important one is probably that in which they decided to hold a nondelivery strike if the government did not meet certain demands. Here is the resolution:
Whereas the increased cost of production of grain caused by higher prices of machinery, higher wages, gas, higher overhead, etc.; and
Whereas the withholding of the final payment on wheat until 1959, works a hardship on the farmer in financing current operations; and
Whereas the wheat contract between Canada and Great Britain previously at $1.55, now $2 per bushel, is a farmer subsidized price, and
Whereas the farmers are also subsidizing domestic consumption; and
Prices Committee

Whereas the farmers should not be asked to subsidize government agreements; and
Whereas price controls have been removed which under present marketing conditions will discourage the production of wheat.
What is that except condemnation in strong terms of the government's agricultural policy by the largest farm body in Alberta, which is fairly representative of what the farmers are thinking. The resolution goes on as follows:
Therefore be it resolved, we recommend, that our board of directors take the necessary steps to call a strike in 1948 unless the following demands are met namely,
1.	Initial price on wheat to be raised to $2 a bushel basis Fort William and Vancouver.
2.	The final payment on participation certificates to be made at the end of each year's operations, and the participation payments for the crop years 1945-46 to be made immediately.
3.	That if the dominion government wishes to sell cheap grain to domestic market or the international field, pending the setting up of the factfinding board and the establishment of parity price, that they subsidize from the dominion treasury, the difference in price between the British wheat agreement and the price paid on the export market.
4.	That the Canadian farmers should be paid the market price on domestic sale of wheat and any necessary subsidy paid by the dominion government.
From that I would say that the farmers are so well satisfied with the present policies of the government that they threaten to strike if these are continued. That is how well satisfied they are. Here is another resolution. Without going into all the "whereases", it is as follows:
Be it resolved that we ask the dominion government to immediately lift the embargo on the shipment of livestock to the United States.
Here is another one with reference to the dominion government's coarse grain policy, which reads in part as follows:
Further be it resolved that this A.F.U. convention severely reprimand the dominion government for this type of decontrol, which allows speculators to make an enormous profit at the expense of the producers. This type of decontrol will not be condoned by this convention.
And so on. So much for the efforts of the Minister of Agriculture made to try to have it appear that the farmers were in favour of his policies. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker,
I would say that the minister's speech was a bare-faced attempt to make black' appear as white, and as such was completely misleading. Perhaps he was only talking for the benefit of some Liberal party members who do not know the situation, in an effort to build himself up for the leadership of his party at the coming convention. I do not know of any other good reason he might have had. Certainly any of the persons who know the situa-

tion would put little stock in what he says. The speech which the minister made is deluding the people who believe him, and also himself; that is particularly true in regard to the statement, which appears at page 806 of Hansard, that the farmers' chief concern is that the Liberal government remain in power, to keep them in a favourable position. I think anyone who is in contact with the farmers at the present time knows that probably the last thing that is concerning them is keeping the Liberal party in power. It is certainly far from their chief concern.
I have always known that the minister was a man with plenty of nerve; but I did not think, particularly after his Lethbridge meeting, that he would have the nerve to make a statement such as that.
He has lots of nerve.
I should like to tell the minister that, as a matter of fact, not ten per cent of the farmers of Alberta would vote for his government and his policies today.
Or in the other provinces either.

A number of former Liberals have told me that. For example, I was talking to a farmer just a few days before I came to Ottawa, and he was full of complaints. He said, "You know, I worked for your Liberal opponent in the last election, and I have voted Liberal all my life; I have worked in nearly every election in the Liberal campaign. But now I am through. I will never cast another Liberal vote." That is the attitude of a large number of former supporters of this government amongst the farmers of the west.
The minister's efforts to misrepresent what the leader of this party said in this debate and at other times are on a par with his statements in regard to the farmers' ideas on his agricultural policies. The same line of misrepresentation, or perhaps what we might call devious argument, has been followed by other government ministers; for example, by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) in his attempt to ridicule our leader's call for a reduction in the sales tax, when he tried to put over the idea that what the leader of the opposition wanted was a reduction in the sales tax on liquor and tobacco. I believe that was an unworthy effort on the right hon. gentleman's part, and that the country will think considerably the less of him because of it.
Then again, the minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) stated that the leader of the opposition and this party had advocated the abolition

Prices Committee
of all controls. When asked to say when and where he said, "Let us be frank and honest about it." I would say that he is the first one who should take his own advice. Let me tell him now that, to my knowledge, this party and its leader have never advocated the abolitio'n of all controls. Some individual members of our party have done so, certainly, but what this party advocated, and what it did pass a resolution about at an annual meeting some two years ago, was "the immediate abolition of all controls on the products of the farm and ranch". That is quite different from the abolition of all controls. If the government had taken that course in their decontrol policy I believe'the whole country would be much better off at the present time. Instead, however, they did just the opposite, and took off practically all controls except those on prices of agricultural products. A great many of our present difficulties have been the result.
Most of the outcry about the rapid increase in living costs has been over the rise in food prices. I suppose this is only natural, because we all have to think of our stomachs and what goes into them at least three times a day. I fear that a considerable number of urban workers blame the high food prices on the greed of the farmers and think that at the present time the farmers are getting too much, without knowing the true situation. It is noteworthy that no one in this house, to my knowledge, and no business or labour leader throughout the country has maintained that the farmer is getting too much. The fact, known to all well-informed persons, is that the farmers are not getting their fair proportion of the national income. If, then, we accept, as I think we must, the fact that the farmer is not getting enough, it follows that prices for farm products are too low rather than too high in comparison with farm costs. Where, then, is the remedy? I believe it is in the bringing down of farm costs, and in lessening the spread between the price the farmer receives and the price the consumer pays.
Farm costs can be brought down in several ways. The first is by increasing production; but the policies of this government have been such as to reduce production rather than to increase it. Farmers have not known where they stand or what the situation is likely to be in the future. They have been at the mercy, as far as prices are concerned, of the Minister of Agriculture and the whims and fancies of this government and its so-called expert advisers. As a result, they have been afraid of the future, afraid to expand their production in many lines. Let me give an example. I happen to be raising some hogs, and have 5849-65J
determined that I can raise five hundred for considerably less per hog than I can raise fifty, and I am taking means to obtain that number. At the same time nearly all my neighbours have been liquidating their hogs. They say to me, "You are taking a terrible gamble. The way Gardiner has been fiddling around with prices of livestock and coarse grains, I would not touch a proposition like yours with a ten-foot pole." That is just an example which illustrates quite well, I think, the lack of confidence that prevails among our farmers at the present time, and, as a result, their unwillingness to plan for increased production. I may add that I am going ahead because, unlike the man whose letter the minister read just before Christmas, and who said he had confidence in God and Gardiner, I have confidence that God and the Canadian people will not permit the Liberal government to continue to mangle agriculture and the whole Canadian economy very much longer.
Another way in which farm costs can be brought down is by the reduction or abolition of the sales tax and1 other indirect taxes on the things farmers must buy in order to produce. If a farmer buys a truck today several hundred dollars of the cost is due to indirect taxes and the mark-up of these taxes which causes them to pyramid1. That money, must, of course, be recovered from the consumer through increased prices. If such farm costs were eliminated farm products could be sold at lower prices and still leave the farmer better off than he is at the present time. Similarly, a reduction in indirect taxes would lessen the spread between the farmers' price and the consumers' price.
These remedies are open to the government now. No committee is required to examine into them and1 take up several months while nothing is done. If the government wishes to bring down food prices let it put into operation policies which will restore the confidence of the farmers and thus increase production. Let it remove or reduce some of the indirect taxes and thus reduce farmers' cost and price spreads. Let it prosecute profiteers, if it can find any. Surely, with all the resources of men and1 machinery in the various government departments and1 agencies, and with the mounted police, they can uncover profiteering much better than a committee of this house. The government already has the power to do this, and to take the necessary punitive measures.
There is one other step the government could take as a temporary measure to relieve immediate hardship. That is, to pay subsidies, on a limited number of essential foods, to
Prices Committee

pensioners and' low income workers. During the pre-Christmas session I suggested that this could be done at practically no administrative cost, in the case of milk for children, by including with the monthly family allowance cheque milk tickets, worth five cents each, for each child for every day in the month. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) pointed out that the same system could1 be used for bread and meat. It could also be used for pensioners, by enclosing the tickets with their monthly cheques. The hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) tried) to ridicule the idea of a milk subsidy toy saying we would) be subsidizing restaurants, people with high incomes, and so forth. But a scheme such as I have mentioned would not subsidize restaurants or any other institutions, or persons with higher incomes, because the amount paid out to them could be collected together with the income tax.
I want to make it clear that I advocate these subsidies only as a temporary expedient to relieve immediate hardship. I do not believe in the general principle of subsidies. In most cases the administrative cost is high and must be paid in higher taxes, so that in the end the goods cost more to the people as a whole than they would otherwise. However, prices are too high for our pensioners, whether they are veterans, old age pensioners or others, and for our lower income workers. Why, then, does the government not take steps; why has it not already taken the steps open to it, to reduce these prices? In my opinion, it has been a case of bad policies, badly mismanaged. The government now seeks to cast the responsibility for its failure on a committee of this house.
There is one thing I am glad the government has done; it has rejected the policy advocated by the C.CJ?., of a general reimposition of price controls. Such a policy is absolutely unsound, I think, for one outstanding reason. It would cut down production, and only by increasing production can prices be brought down in the long run. I should like to say to the C.C.P. and all others who advocate the reimposition of general price controls that you can bring down prices in that way, by law, but you cannot secure production, particularly as far as the farmer is concerned. The only way people will produce is for a profit; that is a truth which should be self-apparent. The only way they would produce otherwise would be under a system of slavery such as one finds under fascism or communism. I believe all will agree that such a system has no place in Canada.

Therefore it seems to me that the advocacy of a system of price control is one which is working against the best interests of this country and of the world as a whole. There is a world shortage of foods; everyone recognizes that. The advocating of a poliey which would increase that shortage is, in my opinion, very closely approaching the criminal.
I have dealt chiefly with agricultural matters and food, because the great clamour is over food prices. However, my remarks are equally applicable to other fields of production, particularly of primary products. I believe the general application of the principles and remedies I have indicated would go far to bring down prices and put our economy on a more sound footing.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in the debate because I consider it is one of the most serious issues which ever faced the Canadian people, and one which should have the serious consideration of all members of the house. I resent the fact that this resolution to set up a committee is placed before us, when through the latest Gallup poll the people of this country demanded action. So far as I am concerned, the resolution brought in by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is nothing short of a smoke screen, as has been pointed out by various members of this group. In my view, anything short of immediate and definite action on the part of the government to prevent the rise in the cost of living would be insufficient at this time.
It seems to me that during the debate many hon. members who, on previous occasions, lent their voices to the government's throwing controls out the window are now taking a different attitude. The hon. member who has just taken his seat has said that his party, as a party, does not believe in complete decontrol. I do not wish to spend much time in refuting what he said; but during the last few years I have listened attentively to addresses by hon. members in his group; and if they do not stand for decontrol, then I wish their leader would come out on behalf of their party and make a speech which would make it unmistakably clear as to the intent of their party in regard to price controls.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) is reported in Hansard for Monday, February 3, 1947, as follows:
The situation is of course further complicated by decontrol in the United States. The lifting of controls there has further complicated the problem of the business community here in various ways and contributed to the situation whereby we have the anomaly of high employ-

nient and scarcity of many necessities. All the indications are that delay from now on in Removing controls will cause constantly increasing difficulties.
And then I quote again from Hansard for April 18, 1947, where the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) states:
The point in my mind here is that the administration of controls, the enforcement of controls, inevitably involves the cutting down of democratic freedom, the lessening of political democracy, in my submission, as well as economic democracy.
And he goes on, speaking of controls:
Indeed it seems to me that at the moment the trouble with the control policy of the government. or the stage at which it has arrived, is that it is only half a plan. It is half control and half decontrol and neither half is working That is why we say the sooner you get rid ot it, the better.
And even the financial critic of the official opposition (Mr. Macdonnell), speaking on the budget, had this to say on May 6, 1947, as reported in Hansard:
At the moment it is particularly unfortunate *that we here who believe in removing controls, and I am one of those, at the present time are at a most unsatisfactory moment, as you might say, from the point of view of the people pi the class of which I am speaking. We are in a period when there is bound to be a certain shaking out of prices, a certain inequality.
Due to the pressure of hon. members to my right, and the people for whom they speak, we have got just what they asked for.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.
